interpretation: Agreement is not accuracy. Disagreements identify rubric boundaries and reviewer uncertainty; medium-confidence independent judgments are not ground truth. The primary assistant agrees with Luna withholding the overtime quotation and additionally questions courtesy-as-Universalism. Independent source reviewers do not unanimously establish errors in the other disputed cases.

method.selected_quotes: Read masked full sources and exact selected quotations before inspecting any case-level evaluator or independent source-agent judgment. Aggregate evaluator counts were known after the user requested status. Medium-confidence acceptance is rubric-based agreement, not human adjudication.
method.sources: Three fresh reviewers each read only their assigned masked full sources and rubric; 41/41/40 groups.

source.journal_entry:
Nothing really happened today worth writing about. Spent most of the morning in back-to-back syncs, the usual Monday chaos of catching up on what slipped over the weekend. Ate lunch at my desk again. Kimchi jjigae from the place downstairs, same order for probably the third week running. I keep meaning to try something different but I'm always too rushed to look at the menu properly.

Had a longer-than-expected call with our warehouse partner in Da Nang about the delayed shipment of syringes. Turned out to be a customs paperwork issue on their end. Nothing dramatic. I walked them through it, helped them resubmit. Could've passed it off to my team but I know that particular contact better and it just went faster to do it myself.

After work I sat on the bus home and watched people through the window for a while. Everyone with their faces in their phones. Some guy was asleep with his mouth open, briefcase sliding off his lap. I thought about how we all just do this every day, the same routes, the same tiredness, and nobody really sees each other. Not a depressing thought exactly, just a passing one. Cooked ramyeon at home, watched half an episode of something, fell asleep on the couch.

My father never let any of us leave Amman until we were married. I accepted that. But I also remember the years I spent wondering what it would have been like to study abroad when I had the chance. I told myself it didn't matter because I had responsibilities. Maybe it didn't matter. Or maybe I just never forgave myself for not pushing harder, and now I'm doing the same thing to her.

source.journal_entry:
My brother Faisal made a comment at Friday lunch about how I'm "still playing student" while his sons are already building careers. His eldest is twenty-six and works at a bank. I smiled and passed the hummus. What I wanted to say was that I spent twenty years running hotel operations so our family name meant something in the hospitality industry, and now I'm doing something for myself, and that should be allowed.

But it wouldn't have been the right moment. My mother was sitting right there, and she gets anxious when Faisal and I disagree. So I stayed quiet, helped clear the plates, and drove home listening to Fairuz with the windows down. The breeze off the hills felt good. I don't need Faisal's approval. I know what I'm doing and why.

Started doing the math again tonight. source.journal_entry:
Had dinner with my daughter Annelies tonight. She asked when I'm going to retire. I told her the same thing I always tell her — when I'm ready. She laughed and said I've been saying that for ten years. She's not wrong.

The truth is, I don't know what I would do. The company isn't just a business, it's the structure of my days. It's where I matter. When I walk into that building, people listen. They need my decisions. At home, Marijke has her garden club and her grandchildren schedule and I'm just another person underfoot. She loves me, I know that, but she doesn't need me the way the company does.

Annelies suggested I mentor young entrepreneurs. The idea of sitting in coffee shops giving advice to twenty-five-year-olds who think they invented disruption makes me want to throw something. I don't want to be an elder statesman. I want to be in the fight.
